final_text: A week passed with no news of Mr. Rochester; ten days, and still he did not come. Mrs. Fairfax said she would not be surprised if he went straight from the Leas to London and from there to the Continent, not showing his face at Thornfield again for a year. He had quite often left just as abruptly and unexpectedly before. When I heard this, I felt a strange chill and sinking at the heart. I was actually letting myself feel a sickening sense of disappointment. But rallying my wits and remembering my principles, I called my emotions to order at once—and it was remarkable how quickly I got over the blunder of supposing Mr. Rochester's movements were something in which I had any reason to take a vital interest. Not that I humbled myself with some slavish sense of inferiority; on the contrary, I simply said—

That is the only connection he seriously recognizes between you and him. So don't make him the object of your fine feelings, your raptures and agonies. He is not of your class: keep to your own, and be too self-respecting to pour out the love of your whole heart, soul, and strength where such a gift is not wanted and would be despised."

final_text: The party was expected to arrive on Thursday afternoon, in time for dinner at six. During the wait, I had no time to nurse fantasies, and I believe I was as active and cheerful as anyone—except Adèle. Still, now and then, something dampened my spirits and threw me back, despite myself, into the territory of doubts, forebodings, and dark speculation. This happened when I chanced to see the third-floor staircase door (which lately had always been kept locked) open slowly and give passage to Grace Poole, in her neat cap, white apron, and handkerchief. I watched her glide along the gallery, her quiet step muffled in a cloth slipper; I saw her look into the busy, upside-down bedrooms, perhaps say a word to the charwoman about the proper way to polish a grate, clean a marble mantelpiece, or remove stains from wallpaper, and then move on. She would descend to the kitchen once a day, eat her dinner, smoke a moderate pipe by the hearth, and go back, carrying her pot of porter for her own private comfort to her gloomy upper rooms. Only one hour out of twenty-four did she spend with the other servants below; the rest of her time was spent in some low-ceilinged, oak-panelled room on the second floor. There she sat and sewed—and probably laughed bleakly to herself—as solitary as a prisoner in a dungeon.

final_text: Afternoon arrived. Mrs. Fairfax put on her best black satin dress, her gloves, and her gold watch, since it was her role to receive the company and show the ladies to their rooms. Adèle, too, insisted on being dressed, though I thought she had little chance of being introduced to the party that day at least. Still, to please her, I let Sophie put her in one of her short, full muslin frocks. For myself, I needed no change; I would not be called from my sanctuary of the schoolroom—for a sanctuary it had now become to me—"a very pleasant refuge in time of trouble."

It was lucky I had secured this food, or she, Sophie, and I—I brought Sophie a share of our meal—would have risked going without dinner entirely. Everyone downstairs was too busy to think of us. Dessert was not carried in until after nine, and at ten, footmen were still running back and forth with trays and coffee cups. I let Adèle stay up much later than usual, since she declared she could not possibly sleep while doors kept opening and closing below and people hurried about. Besides, she added, a message might still come from Mr. Rochester when she was undressed—"et alors quel dommage!"

final_text: As far as her person went, she matched both my picture and Mrs. Fairfax's description point for point. The noble figure, the sloping shoulders, the graceful neck, the dark eyes and black ringlets were all there. But her face? Her face was like her mother's—a youthful, unwrinkled copy: the same low brow, the same strong features, the same pride. It was not, however, quite so sullen and gloomy a pride; she laughed constantly, and her laugh was mocking, as was the habitual expression of her arched and haughty lip.

final_text: At last coffee is brought in, and the gentlemen are summoned. I sit in the shadows—if there are any shadows in this brilliantly lit room; the window curtain half hides me. Again the arch opens; they come. The gentlemen's collective appearance, like the ladies', is imposing. They are all in black; most are tall, some young. Henry and Frederick Lynn are very dashing indeed, and Colonel Dent is a fine soldierly man. Mr. Eshton, the local magistrate, is gentlemanly: his hair is quite white, his eyebrows and whiskers still dark, giving him the air of a distinguished stage father. Lord Ingram, like his sisters, is very tall; like them, he is handsome; but he shares Mary's blank, listless look. He seems to have more length of limb than energy of blood or vigour of mind.

final_text: He comes in last. I am not looking at the arch, yet I see him enter. I try to focus on the netting needles, on the meshes of the purse I am making—I want to think only of the work in my hands, to see only the silver beads and silk threads in my lap. Yet I see his figure plainly, and I cannot help remembering the last time I saw it: just after I had done him what he called an essential service, and he, holding my hand and looking down at my face, had gazed at me with eyes that revealed a heart full and ready to overflow—in whose feelings I had a share. How close I had been to him at that moment! What had happened since to change our positions? Yet now, how distant, how far apart we were! So far apart that I did not expect him to come and speak to me. I did not wonder when, without looking my way, he took a seat on the other side of the room and began talking to some of the ladies.
